scenario.prompt_to_agent:
After an overnight maintenance window, pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports
pings to pc2 (200.1.1.2) are 100% lost, and pc2 reports the same
toward pc1. Yet monitoring shows the router1<->router2 eBGP
session Established with prefixes exchanged, and pc1 can still
ping BOTH of router2's addresses (193.10.11.2 and 200.1.1.1).
Identify what is dropping the traffic.

injection.action: add an iptables FORWARD rule dropping all transit ICMP

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: a DROP rule for protocol icmp sits in router2's FORWARD
  chain, so any ICMP packet router2 must FORWARD (pc1<->pc2 transit
  in either direction) is discarded at the firewall layer. Traffic
  addressed TO router2 itself traverses INPUT, not FORWARD, which
  is why pc1 can still ping 193.10.11.2 and 200.1.1.1. The BGP
  session is TCP, not ICMP, so it stays Established and all
  prefixes remain exchanged -- routing is completely healthy; the
  drop is purely at the packet-filter layer.
Localization: router2
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule for ICMP on
  router2
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP` on router2
scenario.fix_spec:
Remove the DROP rule on router2 -- `iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP`.
Transit pings between pc1 and pc2 succeed again immediately; no routing or
BGP change is needed.

agent.diagnosis_text:
An nftables rule was injected into router2's kernel netfilter FORWARD chain during
the overnight maintenance window. Specifically, the rule `meta l4proto icmp drop`
(visible in both the nft `table ip filter { chain FORWARD }` and the iptables FORWARD
chain as a DROP on protocol 1) silently discards every ICMP packet that router2 is
asked to *forward* — i.e., any ICMP not destined to router2's own addresses.

This explains every observed symptom with precision. Pings from pc1 to pc2 travel
pc1 → router1 → router2 (ingress on eth0, egress on eth1 toward pc2): they hit the
FORWARD hook and are dropped. The reverse path (pc2 → pc1, via router2's eth1 to
eth0) is equally blocked. Because the rule sits in the FORWARD chain and not INPUT,
all traffic *destined to* router2 itself is unaffected: pc1's pings to router2's own
addresses (193.10.11.2 on eth0 and 200.1.1.1 on eth1) pass through the INPUT chain
and succeed normally. The eBGP session between router1 and router2 uses TCP on
router2's local address — again INPUT, not FORWARD — so it stays Established and
continues exchanging prefixes. The packet counter on the drop rule (2 packets, 168
bytes) was freshly incremented by the diagnostic ping, confirming the rule is active
and matching live traffic.

Root cause: a blanket `iptables/nftables FORWARD DROP` rule for ICMP (proto 1) was
added to router2 during the maintenance window, breaking all transit ICMP across the
router while leaving router-terminated sessions intact.

Corrective fix: on router2, remove the offending rule —
`nft delete rule ip filter FORWARD handle <handle>` (or `iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP`)
— and verify end-to-end pings between pc1 and pc2 recover.
